source.title: Kernelized Activation Steering
source.authors: Laziz U. Abdullaev; M. Pham; B. Do; K. Thân; T. Nguyen

record.tranche_reason: The study applies linear contrastive activation addition (ActAdd/DiM) in jailbreak steering and reports harmful-request attack success and utility measures. This is a conceptual test of a difference-in-means direction's behavioral effects, but it does not reproduce the original all-layer ablation or refusal-induction tests.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports ActAdd outcomes on jailbreak prompts and utility measures; those rows are included. The study does not state the ActAdd direction's polarity in the jailbreak setup or give unsteered values for Table 1, so the intervention effect cannot be determined from these outcomes. KAS results are omitted because KAS is the study's new method, not the single DiM direction named in the claim. CAA-style and image-style outcomes concern other target behaviors, not refusal.
record.test_reason: The difference-in-means direction (ActAdd, following Arditi et al.) is a baseline in a comparison of steering methods. The study reports only how each method scores at validation-selected settings. It gives no unsteered ASR, no ablation, no refusal-induction test and no analysis of whether the direction mediates refusal. The ActAdd numbers measure baseline performance in a methods benchmark, not a test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that KAS generalizes DiM (recovered under a linear kernel). They report it outperforms or matches existing steering methods: higher ASR than ActAdd on Gemma and Qwen, equal on Llama, plus gains on CAA behaviours and image style. They draw no conclusion about refusal mediation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear contrastive activation addition as a jailbreak-steering comparator at a validation-selected layer, rather than the original study's refusal-direction ablation/addition tests across layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: The study selects intervention layer and strength on validation data subject to an Alpaca-perplexity cap; exact ActAdd layer and strength values are not stated for Table 1.

fits_no_version.finding: A DiM direction from a single harmful–harmless pair, added at one layer (Gemma L22, Llama L12, Qwen L18), gives mean jailbreak ASR of roughly 69–91% across ten seeds, with higher perplexity than KAS (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A refusal-suppressing DiM direction can be estimated from one contrastive pair, at some cost to fluency.

record.problems: Table 1 gives no unsteered ASR or utility values, preventing assessment of the ActAdd intervention's effect relative to baseline. The text does not specify the polarity of the ActAdd direction for the jailbreak experiment. ActAdd entries in Table 1 have no reported uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows from the included Table 1 ActAdd results were left out. Results for KAS and other steering methods were excluded because they are not the single DiM direction named in the claim; the study's other behavioral tasks do not measure refusal.

untested.parts: Directional ablation, refusal induction on harmless prompts, unsteered baselines, and any claim that the direction mediates refusal. DiM is used only as a single-layer, last-token additive baseline.

record.verdict_notes: The record misstates polarity as 'not stated': §2 defines source A as the behaviour to suppress (harmful) and target B as harmless, v = µB − µA. All rows are ActAdd baseline numbers in a benchmark of a new steering method, so no verdict is given. PPL values are bounded by the validation selection cap and partly reflect selection.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction, test refusal on harmless requests, apply it at every layer and position, or provide unsteered Table 1 comparisons establishing the intervention's behavioral or capability effects.
Whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation adds robustness.
Whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by a dominant direction plus others.
Whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
Transfer of a refusal direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
How refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
